examples: I opened the door. Then a cat came running out.
I took some medicine. Then my headache went away right away.
I called him. Then I was told he had already left.
I went outside. Then I saw that it was snowing.
I turned on the computer. Then it made a strange noise.
fields.explain:
Position: Always comes at the beginning of the second clause, after the first clause ends with a period or comma.
Naturalness: Used when the result happens quickly, right after the preceding action.
Emotional nuance: Can carry a sense of surprise or a new discovery.
No command or volition meaning: Not used in sentences giving a command → only narrates events.
Style: Moderately formal, often used in writing – narratives, diaries, JLPT exam texts.

•
Indicates a result that happens right after the preceding action: "Then…", "As soon as… …".

•
Expresses a result that comes as a surprise, not predicted beforehand: The speaker did not expect B to happen after A.

•
Used to create a natural flow in storytelling: suitable for descriptive and narrative writing.

•
Neutral nuance → somewhat written language: Not used in casual speech between friends (where そしたら、するとさ... is often used).
fields.notes:
•
Appears often in JLPT reading comprehension because of its narrative, descriptive quality.
• Often used to lead to an important discovery in a text: “すると、驚くべき事実が判明した。”
• Never used to introduce an intentional action of the speaker in the second clause. meaning_vi: Immediately, then ～ ⏐ explain: (1) A is the trigger for event B, which happens immediately afterward.
(2) From A, judgment B is drawn. ⏐ examples: 1. 薬を塗った。すると痛みが治まった。
I applied the medicine. Immediately the pain went away.
2. 窓を開けた。すると、蛾が入ってきた。
I was at the door. Immediately a moth flew in.
3. 「私は外出していました。」
「すると、家は誰もいなかったんですね。」
I was out. So there was nobody at home, right?
mistakes: Confusing it with そして: そして only connects information and has no element of surprise.
Using it with volition/command: Writing “すると、行きましょう” is incorrect for this grammar point.
Confusing it with the conversational usage "Well then...": For example, “すると、君はどうする？” has a different meaning.
Omitting the comma after すると: In formal writing, there should be a “、”.
Using it when the two events have no cause-and-effect relationship or closeness in time is logically wrong.

rows: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ってきた。 すると、<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>くなった。
Lists consecutive events, does not emphasize the result.
ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた。 そして、<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>た。
Emphasizes the time sequence – the next action.
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>した。 それから、<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>した。
Well then (indicates the speaker's conclusion/next action)
Used in conversation, different from the grammar point “A。するとB。”
「<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がないよ」「 すると、<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ごう！」

fields.meaning: Speaking of which, that reminds me
examples: The exam is tomorrow, right? That reminds me, I have to buy pencils.
I haven't seen him lately. Oh, that's right, he went to study abroad, didn't he?
Summers in Japan are hot, aren't they? Speaking of which, it got up to 40 degrees last year.
Have you finished your homework? Oh, that reminds me, the teacher said it's due tomorrow.
A new café opened in front of the station. Come to think of it, I still haven't been there.
fields.explain:
Used at the beginning of the second sentence to bring up a new idea related to the previous sentence.
Casual, natural nuance; often used in everyday communication and spoken language.
Often used when the speaker has just remembered something, expressing a natural thought as it is put into words.
Not used in formal documents or official reports (ところで or それにしても can be used instead at a more neutral level).

•
Used for a topic shift based on association: When hearing, saying, or thinking about A, the speaker suddenly remembers a related B.

•
Implies "That reminds me", "Oh, that's right": B is not the main topic, but something that has just suddenly come to mind.

•
Natural, casual: Often used in conversation or narrative writing; a friendly nuance, not too formal.

•
Does not express a direct cause-and-effect relationship: A is not the cause of B, only a reminder.
fields.notes:
• Often appears in JLPT listening conversations, giving a natural feel to the speaker's speech.
• In narrative writing, it serves to lead into recalling the past or related information.
• Flexible translations: "That reminds me", "Oh, that's right", "Oh, right"…
• Must be distinguished from “そうすると” (if so, then), since they sound similar but have completely different meanings. meaning_vi: Speaking of which; Oh, wasn't it ～ ⏐ explain: Used to begin a sentence whose topic is related to something you have remembered. ⏐ examples: 1. 「そういえば、田中君、元気かな？」
Speaking of which, I wonder if little Tanaka is doing well.
2. 「いい家ですね。そういえば、お父様は設計士さんでしたよね。」
What a nice family. Oh, your father is a designer, isn't he?
mistakes: Using it in formal writing: Not suitable in reports or theses → replace with ちなみに or ところで.
Confusing it with そうすると ("if so, then") in logical sentences.
Using it when the two sentences are unrelated: そういえば requires an association or memory triggered by the previous sentence.
Forgetting the comma after そういえば: In written language, write “そういえば、…”.

rows: Used when you suddenly remember something related.
そういえば、<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだ。
A topic shift, but not necessarily based on association.
ところで、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>は？
Expresses a strong emotion about what came before.
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>いね。それにしても<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>異常<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>だ。
Expresses a conclusion drawn from the previous information (logic).
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>か。そうすると<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だね。

examples: I contacted him. But I still haven't gotten a reply.
I thought I'd be able to go tomorrow. But then I suddenly came down with a fever…
The test was easy, wasn't it? Actually, I couldn't do any of it.
I was planning to go on a trip, but it got canceled because of a typhoon.

Have you finished your homework yet?
―Well, actually, I haven't even done half…
fields.explain:
Position: Comes at the beginning of clause B, after a complete sentence A.
Nuance: Soft, with a slight sense of regret, reluctance, or a reason that is hard to say.
Level of casualness: Used a lot in everyday conversation; rarely used in formal written language.
Trailing off: It can be left hanging after それが to create a sense of hesitation or difficulty saying something directly.

•
Expresses something contrary to expectation: The fact in clause B differs from or is the opposite of what was expected from clause A.

•
Used to shift the idea with gentle emotion: carries the nuance of "you'd think so, but it isn't", "but in reality…".

•
Used to explain a difficult reason / to decline tactfully: When the speaker hesitantly gives a reason why something cannot be done.

• Common in natural conversation; has a justifying, soft-contrast quality, unlike でも (which has a more direct nuance).
fields.notes:
• Often accompanied by expressions of feeling and hesitation to reduce the degree of negation or refusal.
• Can be used to answer when asked directly about something that is hard to answer straight.
• In spoken language, it can be stretched to “それがね…” to open an explanation. meaning_vi: (1) (As for) that, ～, but ～
(2) But ～ ⏐ explain: (1) Used when talking about an unexpected result.
(2) Expresses a result different from the plan or expectation in the previous sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 「お嬢さん、もう大学をご卒業されましたでしょう？」
「それが、まだなんですよ。」
Your daughter has already graduated from university, hasn't she? Well, not yet, actually.
2. たばこをやめると誓った。それが、たった三日でまた吸ってしまった。
I swore I would quit smoking. But after only 3 days I ended up smoking again.
mistakes: Confusing it with それで: それで = "so, therefore…", while それが = "and yet…", contrary to expectations.
Using it in overly formal writing: Not suitable; replace with しかし or ただし in argumentative writing.
Using it when B does not contrast with A: それが requires clause B to differ from what is expected from A.
Omitting clause A: Previous context is always needed for それが to make sense.

rows: Soft; often used to decline or explain.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりだった。 それが、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けなくて。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。でも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けない。
The reality is completely contrary to what was expected, often a strong surprise.
<ruby>勝<rt>か</rt></ruby>つと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った。ところが<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けた。
Talks about the result that follows; no contrastive meaning.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。 それで<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>した。

examples: He failed many times. Even so, he didn't give up.
It was raining hard. Even so, the audience didn't leave.
I warned him. Even so, he made the same mistake.
This job is tough, you know. Are you still going to do it?
I gave it my all. Even so, I couldn't win.
fields.explain:
Position: Comes at the beginning of clause B, after clause A ends with a period or comma.
The two clauses must be in an opposing relationship: A makes us think B will not happen, but in reality B still happens.
Nuance: Emotional – surprise, disappointment, admiration, perseverance.
Style: Used in both conversation and written language; neutral level of formality.

•
Expresses concession + contrast: Even though A is an obstacle, a difficulty, or something that makes B unlikely, result B still happens.

•
Emotional implication: Often carries a nuance of perseverance, surprise, disappointment, or praise (for still doing B despite A).

•
Natural translations: "Even so…", "But…", "Nevertheless…", "Even then…".

•
Different from それが・それで・そこで: それでも emphasizes the strong contrast between expectation (from A) and reality (B).
fields.notes:
• Often used in narratives, emotional statements, and expressions of volition.
• Often used together with emphatic words such as それでもなお (but still…) and それでもやっぱり.
• Flexible translations: "But", "Nevertheless", "Even then…", "And yet…".
• Appears often in the reading and listening sections of JLPT N3–N2. meaning_vi: However, even so ～ ⏐ explain: Expresses an opinion or result opposite to situation A in the preceding clause. ⏐ examples: 1. 外は大雨だ。それでも出かけないといけない。
It's raining heavily outside. Even so, I have to go out.
2. みんなに反対されている。それでも私は彼と結婚したい。
Everyone is against it. Even so, I want to marry him.
mistakes: Confusing it with それで: それで = "so, therefore…", while それでも = "even so…".
No contrasting element: Incorrect if clauses A and B are not opposed, or if A is not an obstacle to B.
Using it in overly formal writing: Not suitable in research or reports → use しかしながら.
Omitting the comma after それでも in written language: write “それでも、…”.

rows: Emphasizes that B happens in spite of A.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。 それでも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Emphasizes an emotion of surprise or complaint.
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>いね。 それにしても<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>異常<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>だ。
Colloquial, simple; does not emphasize overcoming an obstacle.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。 でも<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい。
Used when reality is contrary to expectation; somewhat hesitant.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。 それが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けなくなった。

examples: I'm off tomorrow. —Then let's go out together.
It's already sold out. —Then we should have reserved one.
You don't have a car? Then let's go by bus.
This plan is high-risk. In that case, let's consider an alternative.
You're not feeling well? Then don't push yourself.
fields.explain:
Usually comes at the beginning of a reply, together with a suggestion/solution/concession.
Not used simply for contrast; there must be a conditional relationship "if A is true, then B...".
Casual: だったら／じゃ(あ); polite: それならば／それでは.

• Meaning: "If so, then / in that case...", used when you take in information A and then decide on/suggest B.
• Conversational function: responding, moving on to a solution, giving advice or a new condition.
• Formality: neutral in conversation; それならば is more polite; だったら/じゃ(あ) are more casual.
fields.notes:
• Suitable in negotiation/problem-solving because it shows a flexible response.
• Can be used with a command/advice: それなら、やめたほうがいい。
• In polite emails, prefer それでは／それならば.
mistakes: Using それなら for pure contrast (use しかし/だが instead) → wrong function.
Mixing it up with それでは: in natural conversation, それなら is neutral; それでは is formal/used for guiding through procedures.
B lacks the quality of "reacting to A" → the sentence becomes disjointed.

rows: More casual than それなら
If so, then; well then (opening/closing a section)
More polite; also used to move to the next step in a presentation
それでは<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
A grammatical element attached directly to nouns/verbs/adjectives

examples: I don't want to go. I mean, I'm tired.
Today's impossible. Because I have plans.
How would I know that? I mean, nobody told me.
Don't be angry. I only meant it as a joke.
He's kind, you know. Because he always helps me.
fields.explain:
Casual spoken language, usually in conversations between friends/family.
Adding んだもん／もの strengthens the nuance of self-justification/cuteness; から is more neutral.
Avoid using it to open formal texts; if a standard reason is needed, use ので／ため／だから.

• Explains a reason based on emotion/mild excuse-making: "It's because… you know".
• Not meant for strict logical argument, but to show personal feelings and self-justification.
• Usually comes at the beginning of the sentence, followed by a comma; S2 is the reason clause.
fields.notes:
• The form “だってさ” is used when quoting rumors/what others said, not to give a reason.
• In polite conversation, you can switch to: 申し訳ありません。忙しいので…。 (avoid だって).
• Children and women often use ～んだもん／もの; adult men tend to use it less to avoid sounding childish. explain: A spoken-language way of saying 「なぜなら」 「なぜかというと」 「どうしてかというと」 ⏐ examples: 1. 「何を怒ってるの？」「だって、約束を破ったじゃないか。」
What are you angry about? Isn't it because you broke your promise?
2. 「テストの点、よかったんだって？」
「うん。だってやさしかったんだもん。」
I heard you got a good score on the test? Yes, that's because it was easy.
mistakes: Using だって in essays/business letters → not suitable; replace with ので／ため／理由は～です.
Confusing the conjunction だって with the particle だって meaning "even": look at the position (beginning of a sentence vs. after a noun).
Combining だって with です／ます creates a style mismatch: avoid “だって、忙しいですから。” in formal situations.
In listening comprehension, だって + んだもん signals emotion, not an objective reason.

rows: だって、<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>いんだもん。
More neutral, can be used in writing
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。だから、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいので<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できません。
Not a conjunction; comes after a noun

examples: This system will be reviewed starting next year. That's because it no longer fits the current situation.
SDGs means the Sustainable Development Goals.
It seems he won't attend. That's because we just heard from him that he isn't feeling well.
This medicine isn't covered by insurance. That's because it hasn't been approved yet.
A "black company" is a company that forces excessive burdens on its workers.
fields.explain:
A comma usually follows というのは to separate the explanation.
When explaining a reason, end with からだ／ためだ to make the cause-and-effect relationship clear.
Used for definitions: XというのはYのことだ → concise, formal, often seen in textbooks and articles.
Colloquial: っていうのは → softer, suitable for conversation and blogs.
Not used at the end of a sentence; it is always followed by an explanatory clause.

• Explanation/definition: A way to "clarify" the content just stated in the previous sentence. Often used with のことだ／ということだ.
• Giving a reason: States a cause that serves as a conclusion for the preceding clause. Often accompanied by からだ／ためだ to settle the reason.
• Scope of reference: というのは usually refers directly to the whole previous sentence (A)。この/その＋話/件 can be used to make this clear.
• Nuance: Logical, objective; used a lot in newspapers, discussions, reports, and presentations.
fields.notes:
• Instead of からだ, わけだ/ためだ/にほかならない can be used to strengthen the nuance of a conclusion.
• If the explanation is long, break up the sentence and use a comma after というのは for readability.
• In spoken language, というのは can take the contracted form つーのは/てのは (very colloquial); avoid using these in the JLPT.
mistakes: Confusing it with ということは: というのは explains A; ということは infers B from A.
Forgetting からだ/ためだ when giving a reason makes the sentence lack conclusive force.
Putting というのは at the end of a sentence (incorrect); it must be followed by an explanatory clause.
Writing it without a comma: “というのはB…” is still acceptable, but a comma should be used for clarity in reading exams.

rows: Refers to the previous sentence; often with からだ/ということだ
なぜなら／なぜかというと
Introduces a reason directly; usually ends with からだ
Rephrases the same content; not really giving a reason
B does not explain A but is inferred from A
Usually used right after a term; no previous sentence needed

fields.meaning: What is called…, the thing named…
examples: 「デジカメ」 is a shortened way of saying "digital camera."

What does 「カクテイ」 mean when talking about trains?
It's a train that stops at every station.
fields.explain: Used when you want to define or explain a thing or matter (with the phrase to be defined as the subject)

examples: You don't need to apologize.
There's no need to come. Sending it by mail is fine.
fields.explain: Used when you want to tell the other person that they do not necessarily have to do a certain action. It is acceptable even if that action is not done.

fields.meaning: Expresses taking ~ as the standard for evaluation. Judging from ~, in terms of ~
examples: Judging from Kenta's personality, ...
Judging from Kenta's personality, he probably can't clearly say "I like you" to the person he likes.
Judging from that person's attitude, they must dislike me.
fields.notes: Indicates a clue for a judgment. Also expressed as 「からして」 or 「からみて」.（９０）

fields.meaning:
「～がいちばん…。」客観的な事実ではなくて、話者が主観的に言うときに使う。
Used when the speaker wants to express their subjective impression rather than an objective fact.
fields.connection: N + くらい/ぐらい/ほど + ～はない（～ is the most, subjective）
examples: Nobody loves animals as much as Lee.
I think there's nothing as enjoyable as cooking.
Oh no, there's another kanji test tomorrow. There's nothing I hate more than tests.
I've never felt as anxious as when I found out I was sick two years ago.
fields.explain:
Used to elevate the degree of a thing, matter, or person.
Affirms that apart from that thing, matter, or person, there is nothing equivalent that could replace it
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: 「ほど．．．はない」expresses the meaning of the structure「～が一番．．．だ」. There is nothing as ~ as ~
examples: 1. ①　ニューヨークほど（は）寒くない
Not as cold as New York
2. ②　A大学の入学試験は、B大学の試験ほど難しくない。
The entrance exam of University A is not as difficult as the exam of University B.
3. ③　ロンドンはニューヨークほどは寒くない。
London is not as cold as New York.
4. ④　今日は思ったほど暑くない。
Today is not as cold as I thought.
──────
1. ①　サッカーほどおもしろいスポーツはない
There is no sport more interesting than soccer.
2. ②　健太ほど忘れっぽい人はいない。
Nobody is more forgetful than Kenta
3. ③　人の自慢話を聞くことほど退屈なことはない。
There is nothing more boring than listening to other people brag about themselves.
meaning_vi: As … as that, there is none….
examples: 1. 彼女くらい親切な人はいない。
There is no one as kind as her
2. 今年ほど雪の降った年はなかった。
There has never been a year with as much snow as this year
